procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 16.08.2018 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Petition No. 4463 of 2018, discharging the respondent from offenses under Section 13(1)(e) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Criminal Revision Petition No. 287 of 2013: Respondent (original petitioner-accused) filed a Criminal Revision Petition before the High Court after the trial court dismissed his application challenging the sanction. The High Court disposed of the petition on 05.07.2013, directing the trial court to consider the documents made available by the respondent during the investigation and produced by the prosecution with the chargesheet, while framing the charge without being influenced by the order dated 01.12.2013.
2. Criminal Petition No. 4463 of 2018: The respondent filed a Criminal Petition under Section 482 of CrPC before the High Court after the trial court dismissed his third application seeking discharge. The High Court allowed the petition on 16.08.2018, discharging the respondent from the offenses charged.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, State of Karnataka Lokayukta Police, approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 16.08.2018 in Criminal Petition No. 4463 of 2018. The Supreme Court is considering whether the High Court could reverse the findings of the Special Court regarding the validity of sanction in a petition filed under Section 482 of the CrPC, considering the bar in sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.
It will be open for the respondent to raise the issue of validity of sanction if he desires to do so, in accordance with law at the ﬁnal stage of arguments in the trial.
Special Judge is directed to proceed with the trial from the stage it had stopped, in accordance with the law and as expeditiously as possible.

issue.issue_text: Whether an interlocutory application seeking discharge in the midst of trial would be maintainable?

facts: The accused filed an application for discharge in the middle of the trial.
This was after the Special Judge had already taken cognizance of the case and framed charges against the accused.
The trial had proceeded to the point where the prosecution had examined 17 witnesses.
The accused had previously raised the issue of the validity of the sanction for prosecution but had not pressed the matter, allowing the court to proceed with framing the charges.
law: Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, states that once cognizance is taken and charges are framed, the trial should not be stayed or scuttled.

The appropriate stages for an accused to raise an issue like the validity of a sanction are: 1) when the court takes cognizance, 2) when charges are being framed, or 3) during the final arguments at the conclusion of the trial.
application: The Court applied the bar from Section 19(3) of the Act, reasoning that since the trial was already in progress after the framing of charges, it could not be interrupted by an application for discharge.
The Court noted that the accused had a prior opportunity to argue for discharge before the charges were framed but chose not to.
Therefore, filing an application for discharge in the middle of the trial was procedurally improper and not maintainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an interlocutory application seeking discharge in the midst of a trial is not maintainable. The Court reasoned that once charges are framed and the trial has begun, it cannot be stayed or scuttled. The accused's only remaining opportunity to raise such issues is during the final arguments of the trial.

issue.issue_text: At what stages of proceedings can an accused raise the issue with regard to the validity of the sanction?

law.provision: Section 19(1) forbids a court from taking cognizance of an offence against a public servant without a valid prior sanction.
law.explanation: This section establishes the legal requirement for a sanction before a prosecution can begin.

These sub-sections limit the power of an appellate or revisional court to reverse a finding or sentence due to an error in the sanction. Such a reversal is only permitted if the error has resulted in a "failure of justice," and the court must consider whether the objection to the sanction could and should have been raised at an earlier stage.

application.description: The Court identified three specific stages during the trial process where an accused can challenge the validity of the sanction.
These stages are: 1) When the court first takes cognizance of the offence. 2) When the charge is being framed. 3) During the final arguments after the trial is complete.

The Court noted that while it is best to raise the issue at the earliest opportunity, it is not an absolute bar to raising it later. However, it held that once cognizance is taken and the charge is framed, an accused cannot file an interlocutory application for discharge in the middle of the trial on this ground. In that situation, the accused must wait until the final arguments.

The Court also clarified that the issue can be raised in post-trial proceedings like an appeal, revision, or confirmation. However, the power of these higher courts is restricted by Section 19(3) and (4) of the Act, meaning they can only intervene if the invalid sanction has caused a failure of justice.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an accused can raise the issue of the validity of a sanction at three main stages during the trial: when the court takes cognizance, when the charge is framed, or at the final arguments. The issue can also be raised in an appeal or revision, but the higher court's power to interfere is limited to cases where the error has caused a failure of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court in a criminal petition filed under Section 482 of the CrPC could reverse the findings recorded by the Special Court with regard to the validity of sanction, ignoring the bar contained in sub-section (3) read with sub-section (4) of Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988?

facts: The accused-respondent filed three separate applications before the Special Court seeking discharge from the case, each time challenging the validity of the sanction for prosecution.
The second application was specifically withdrawn by the accused, who requested the court to proceed with framing the charges.
The trial commenced, and the prosecution examined 17 witnesses.
After this, the accused filed a third application, again challenging the sanction. The Special Judge dismissed this application, recording a specific finding that the sanction was proper and valid.
The accused challenged this dismissal in the High Court through a petition under Section 482 of the CrPC.
The High Court reversed the Special Judge's finding and allowed the petition.
law: Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, places a specific bar on higher courts.

It states that no finding, sentence, or order passed by a Special Judge shall be reversed or altered by a court in appeal, confirmation, or revision on the ground of any error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction.
This bar has one exception: a higher court can interfere, but only if it is of the opinion that a "failure of justice has in fact been occasioned" by the defective sanction.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Special Judge had recorded a clear finding that the sanction was valid when dismissing the third discharge application.
The High Court, while exercising its power under Section 482 CrPC (which was in the nature of a revision), reversed this specific finding.
However, the High Court did so without recording any opinion or reason as to how the alleged error in the sanction had led to a "failure of justice."

By reversing the Special Judge's order without satisfying the mandatory condition of finding a failure of justice, the High Court acted in direct contravention of the specific bar contained in Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's approach, holding that it could not reverse the Special Court's findings on the validity of the sanction. The High Court was bound by the specific bar in Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and was legally prohibited from interfering with the Special Court's order without first concluding that a failure of justice had actually occurred due to the alleged error in the sanction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an interlocutory application seeking discharge in the midst of trial would be maintainable?
appellant_arguments: An application for discharge is not maintainable in the middle of a trial, especially after the prosecution has already examined 17 witnesses.
The respondent had previously filed and then explicitly not pressed an application for discharge, requesting the court to frame charges, which led to the trial commencing.
respondent_arguments: An interlocutory application for discharge is maintainable during the trial if it is based on a fundamental defect, such as an invalid sanction order.

arguments.issue_text: At what stages of proceedings can an accused raise the issue with regard to the validity of the sanction?
appellant_arguments: The respondent waived their right to challenge the sanction's validity by not pressing the issue before the charges were framed and by allowing the trial to proceed to the examination of 17 witnesses.
According to Section 19(4) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, the court must consider whether the objection to sanction 'could and should have been raised at an earlier stage'.
respondent_arguments: The validity of a sanction order is a crucial issue that can be raised at any stage of the proceedings, including during the trial, as it goes to the root of the court's jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court in a criminal petition filed under Section 482 of the CrPC could reverse the findings recorded by the Special Court with regard to the validity of sanction, ignoring the bar contained in sub-section (3) read with sub-section (4) of Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988?
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have entertained the petition under Section 482 of the CrPC, as it was in the nature of a revision application.

The High Court's decision to reverse the trial court's findings is barred by the clear and unambiguous language of sub-section (3) read with sub-section (4) of Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
The High Court failed to consider that any error in sanction cannot be a ground for reversal unless it has resulted in a failure of justice and that the objection should have been raised earlier.
respondent_arguments: The High Court has inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to intervene and quash proceedings if there is a fundamental error, such as an invalid sanction granted by an incompetent authority.
The trial court's dismissal of the application was incorrect, justifying the High Court's intervention to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act prohibits a higher court from reversing an order of a Special Judge on the ground of any defect, omission, or irregularity in the sanction. This prohibition does not forbid a Special Judge from passing an order at any stage of the proceedings holding that the prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid sanction.
obiter: When an appellate or revisional court examines whether an error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction has caused a failure of justice, it must have regard to whether the objection could and should have been raised before the trial court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's intervention under Section 482 CrPC to reverse the Special Court's finding on the validity of a sanction order mid-trial was legally impermissible. Such a reversal by a higher court is explicitly barred by Section 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, which prohibits an appellate or revisional court from reversing a trial court's order on the ground of an error in sanction unless it finds that a "failure of justice" has been occasioned, a determination which was neither pleaded by the respondent nor opined upon by the High Court.
legal_tests_applied: The "Failure of Justice" Test (Section 19(3), PC Act): A finding, sentence, or order passed by a Special Judge shall not be reversed or altered by a higher court on the ground of any error, omission, or irregularity in the sanction, unless that court is of the opinion that "a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby".

The "Timeliness of Objection" Consideration (Section 19(4), PC Act): When determining if a failure of justice has occurred, the appellate or revisional court must "have regard to the fact whether the objection could and should have been raised at any earlier stage in the proceedings."
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the respondent had irrevocably waived the right to challenge the sanction's validity. By explicitly permitting the respondent to raise the issue again at the final stage of the trial, the court affirmed that the right to challenge sanction before the trial court is not permanently extinguished by a failure to press it at the initial stage.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's argument that the validity of a sanction can be raised at any stage before the trial court. It reasoned that the prohibition in Section 19(3) of the PC Act applies to higher courts interfering with a trial court's order, but it "does not forbid a Special Judge from passing an order at whatever stage of the proceedings holding that the prosecution is not maintainable for want of a valid order sanctioning the same."
policy_considerations: The legislature disfavors "axing down the proceedings or to direct repetition of the whole proceedings afresh" due to procedural errors like a defective sanction, instead imposing a high bar for intervention.

The rationale underlying Section 19(3) and (4) is that once a trial has proceeded to a conclusion, the findings "should not be lightly interfered with by the appellate or the revisional court simply because there was some omission, error or irregularity in the order sanctioning the prosecution," unless a substantive failure of justice is demonstrated.
